summary: Mission Mooquake is a web-based, 2D isometric game made for kids between ages 7-12. They will play as an astronaut who gets hit with a moonquake and has one week to repair equipment, gather data, and prepare their home base before a solar storm hits. Players will manage oxygen, power, energy, and radiation shielding while earning knowledge points through minigames. The minigames are meant to mimic tasks astronauts perform while in space or in NASA’s research centers, such as planting seismometers, growing plants, testing soil, and communicating with Earth. Skipping sleep or meals lowers research output to show the importance of maintaining proper routine while in space. Using power on LEDs grows more food but leaves less for radiation shields. The game utilizes NASA research and datasets. OSDR was used to get data on how plants are grown using the Veggie station. Later on, DONKI will be used to provide live weather data that can be used to create solar flares that will decide if the player levels up. Our project aims to create real world impact by allowing kids to not only learn about space in a fun and interactive way, but also gain high-stakes decision-making experience.
details:
Our project is based on the NASA challenge, “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” It is a web-based application that allows users to interact with an astronaut character using simple controls, such as the arrow keys and cursor. Designed for children ages 7–12, the game introduces players to concepts about space and shares fun, educational facts along the way. Presenting this information in a game format makes learning more interactive and enjoyable, encouraging children to actively engage with the material rather than simply reading about it. Ultimately, our goal is to spark curiosity and inspire young learners to explore and learn more about space.

Our project is built using the React and Next.js frameworks. The frontend uses TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and PixiJS for the isometric WebGL game renderer, along with SVG and browser APIs to support interactive UI elements and graphics. The backend is powered by Next.js route handlers. Since gameplay runs locally in the browser, the application does not require a database or a separate backend service.

One of the most creative aspects of our project is its use of an isometric perspective to create an engaging gameplay experience. We also designed custom visual assets and icons specifically for the game, making the interface more appealing and approachable for younger audiences. Throughout development, our team considered several factors, including the target audience's age, interests, existing knowledge of space, and the types of space-related facts that would be most engaging and interesting to children. These considerations guided our research and helped us select educational topics that are both informative and enjoyable for our intended audience.
